### ST technologies

The types of technology used to generate spatial transcriptomics data are generally categorized as {{< glossary "Sequence-based technologies" display = "sequencing-based" >}} or {{< glossary "Image-based technologies" display = "image-based" >}} and lie across two inverse spectra: Molecular {{< glossary Resolution >}} and Cellular Resolution. Sequencing-based technologies typically provide a whole {{< glossary Transcriptome display = "transcriptome" >}} view (broad molecular resolution), but not at a single-cell or sub-cellular resolution -- instead at a Region of Interest (ROI) or {{< glossary Spot display = '"spot"' >}} resolution (where a "spot" is made up of tens to hundreds of cells.) In other words, sequencing-based technologies provide low precision / cellular resolution. In contrast, image-based technologies typically provide data for a panel-based subset or a limited selection of the transcriptome (in other words, narrow molecular resolution). However, image-based technologies provide data at a single-cell or even sub-cellular resolution (high precision cellular resolution). Due to this, researchers may first collect spatially-informed gene expression data with a sequencing-based technology for initial hypothesis generation to identify a specific region of interest in a tissue or specific genes to probe where greater cellular resolution would be beneficial, and then follow-up with generating a higher cellular resolution spatially-informed dataset using an image-based technology. @Kwon_etal_2026 is a study posted to bioRxiv recently where the researchers did just this: first using a sequencing-based technology followed by an image-based technology as complementary spatial transcriptomic approaches to study the impacts of {{< glossary Schizophrenia display = "schizophrenia (SCZ)" >}} within the {{< glossary "laminar domains" >}}, microenvironments, and cell types of {{< glossary "Postmortem samples" display = "postmortem samples" >}} from the human {{< glossary "Dorsolateral prefrontal cortext" display="dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC)" >}}. 


```{r echo = FALSE, fig.align = 'center', out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Visium and Xenium provide spatially informed mRNA expression at different molecular and cellular scales. The molecular resolution of Visium, a sequencing-based technology is high because it gives a view of the whole transcriptome. The Molecular resolution of Xenium, an image-based technology, is low because it gives a view of a only a limited number of genes from a specified panel. On the other hand, the cellular resolution of Visium is lower than that of Xenium. Visium does not provide a single-cell resolution. Rather its spot-level resolution can have multiple cells represented. Xenium provides single-cell or even sub-cellular resolution."}

|:--------------------|:--------------:|:--------------------:|:--------------------:|
|Sequencing-based     | {{< glossary Visium >}}, GeoMx, Slide-seq | Broad; whole transcriptome | Low; Near single-cell but typically spots with tens to hundreds of cells represented |
|Image-based          | {{< glossary "Xenium" >}}, CosMx, MERFISH | Limited; panel of specific genes | High; single- or sub-cellular resolution |

### Uses of ST data

Spatially-informed gene expression data is useful for investigating differential expression in multiple contexts: overall transcript abundance, cell-type specific expression, and spatial distribution of expression.

## The human nervous system

The human nervous system allows humans to receive, process, and communicate signals based on input from their surroundings. The nervous system is made up of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord which direct the understanding and communication of received signals to the rest of the nervous system[@Coon_Mitterer_2015].

Neurons are a specialized cell type necessary for the communication of these signals within the nervous system and they are cells with an abnormal shape. The body of the cell has the nucleus with branch-like extensions called dendrites which receive signals. Each neuron also has slender projection off of the body of cell called an axon which transmits signals to other cells. The axon has a insulating layer called a myelin sheath to help with signal transduction. Nerves within the nervous system are made up of bundles of axons from multiple neurons[@Coon_Mitterer_2015]. 

```{r echo = FALSE, fig.align = 'center', out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Diagram from NIH Bio Art showing a neuron specifically highlighting its cell body with the nucleus, the dendrites branching off of the cell body and the myelin sheath covered axon slender offshoot."}

```

The brain has several other specialized cells such as astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes provide the myelin sheath insulation around the axons of neurons.

## What is the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex?

***

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is a specific part of the frontal lobe of the cerebral cortex of the brain. The cerebral cortex is the outer layer in the upper part of the brain where cognition is localized. It's a twisted and folded structure made up of gray matter (spongy tissue made up mostly of the neuronal cell bodies) which sits atop white matter (made up of the neuronal axons and oligodendrocytes). The prefrontal cortex is also known as the "prefrontal area" and is found in the front and top of the frontal lobe. The dorsolateral portion of the prefrontal cortex is towards the top and side of the prefrontal cortex. The dlPFC roughly corresponds with Brodmann area 46 (BA46) and is invovled in exectuve functioning and cognitive control, contributing to working memory and emotional regulation [@Kirby_etal_2024].

## Why collect samples from the dlPFC?

***

Given that the dlPFC has been implicated in cases of schizophrenia, specifically cognitive symtpoms, researchers commonly study this area of the brain for schizophrenia research. Brain imaging studies *in vivo* (MRI, PET, etc.) do not need to collect samples because such imaging can be done with research participants [@Keshavan_etal_2020]. To study the molecular biochemistry and omics of this brain region on a larger scale than is possible with live imaging, however, postmortem samples need to be collected.


## Why is spatially-informed gene expression data necessary?

***

The dlPFC has several laminar domains or layers, each of which seems to have its own structure and molecular signature (e.g., cell composition, gene expression patterns, morphology, connectivity, etc.), and therefore, likely, a unique role in cognitive function. Originally introduced in the early 1900s [@Zilles_2018], these layers have been confirmed throughout the years with recent single cell and spatial transcriptomics studies using a data-driven approach in describing them rather than manually annotating them [@Maynard_etal_2021; @Huuki-Myers_etal_2024].

```{r echo = FALSE, fig.align = 'center', fig.alt = 'Diagram showing the laminar domains within a slice of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.'}
ottrpal::include_slide("https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk/edit?slide=id.h46301d28624b2de3_0_49#slide=id.h46301d28624b2de3_0_49")
```

<detail><summary>Laminar domains in the dlPFC </summary>

* L1:
* L2:
* L3:
* L4:
* L5:
* L6:
* WM: White matter

</details>

Given this, spatially-informed gene expression data is beneficial not just for studying how gene expression may differ in abundance between neurotypical cases and cases with diagnosed schizophrenia, and not just for querying if cell types show differences in expression or composition between cases, but also to query if there might be differences among these layers, a point discussed by @Maynard_etal_2021. In this way, spatial transcriptomics acts as a hypothesis generation tool either to find candidate patterns that can be assayed further or for initial investigation into mechanisms to interpret previously identified risk genes.
